title: How To Make Your Routines More Effective
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies a single, rarely-used adjustment that can significantly boost the value of well-taught classroom routines: making them longer, either by combining several separate routines into one extended procedure or by deliberately adding extra, even quirky, steps to a standalone routine. He is emphatic that routines must run entirely on the teacher's 'go' signal without any input, narration, or guidance once taught, since stepping in nullifies the routine's benefit and shifts responsibility back onto the teacher. He argues that lengthening a routine — for example, combining entry, homework turn-in, and starting the first assignment into a single sequence, or adding a fist bump and a silly dance step before lining up — gives students more sustained practice attacking a self-directed challenge, which builds efficiency, purpose, motivation, and self-sufficiency that transfers to their broader academic responsibilities.
points: Once taught, routines must run entirely on a 'go' signal with zero teacher input; stepping in to narrate or guide nullifies their value.
Combining multiple separate routines (entry, homework turn-in, starting work) into one longer sequence increases their instructional value.
Adding extra, even nonsensical or playful steps to a standalone routine (a fist bump, a silly dance step) still lengthens and strengthens it.
Longer, self-directed routines give students more sustained practice with independence, which builds efficiency, purpose, and self-sufficiency.
The benefits of longer routines are described as transferring to students' broader academic responsibilities, not just the routine itself.
quotes: This is key. The teacher merely gives a “Go” signal . The students carry out the routine all on their own.
If you step in to remind, guide, or narrate, it nullifies the routine’s value and shifts responsibility back to the teacher, which is the last thing you want.
So instead of having one routine for entering the classroom, another for turning in homework, and a third for beginning the first assignment of the day, you would splice them together.
For example, you might have your students circle to the back of the room first, fist bump a friend, and then do a jig on an X next to your desk before lining up.
The practice makes them more efficient, purpose-driven, motivated, and self-sufficient. It puts more weight on their shoulders.
